---
title: "After you have your level"
description: "The rules that keep a level honest: disagreement, time pressure, Business Critical work, and recording the decision."
---

*Phase 1, engagement and scoping. [Where this sits in the
lifecycle](../04-analytical-lifecycle/index.qmd).*

You have scored the six impact dimensions and the six likelihood dimensions and read your level
off the grid. [Back to the decision](index.qmd) if you have not.

This page is everything that keeps that level honest: what to do when somebody disagrees with it,
what to do when there is not enough time to deliver it, what changes if the work is Business
Critical, how to record it, and why the instrument is built the way it is.

## Why the level is scored rather than judged

Assurance is proportionate to the work, and what makes a piece of analysis need more of it is a
known list: the risks of its intended use, its type and complexity, the novelty of the approach, the
importance of the issue, how central it is to the decision, the precision required, and the resource
available.[^src-aqua-book-table-3-1] Scoring that list is how two people reach the same answer
independently, and how the answer can be looked up six months later.

The scales are on the [previous page](index.qmd), shortened to the deciding phrases from the
decision sheet's own wording. **Where the two ever differ, the sheet governs.**
[Section 13](/guidance/13-getting-help/index.qmd) is how to report it so this page can be corrected.

## The eight types of analytical model

Where your work is a model rather than a one-off analysis, it will be one of eight types. The list
is the one the government modelling guidance uses, and it is worth being able to place your own
work in it.

**Policy simulation**: to better understand the options that drive a decision, by estimating the
likely cost and impact of each choice before it is made.

**Forecasting**: to predict the future and inform today's choices. Projections of demand, volume or
cost that let future pressures be understood while there is still time to act on them.

**Financial evaluation**: to better understand future liabilities or costs, where a commitment made
now is paid for over many years.

**Procurement and commercial evaluation**: for the letting and management of large contracts, and
to ensure value for money.

**Planning**: to make workforce and capacity decisions which affect the delivery of future
services.

**Science based**: to better understand and simulate the physical environment, in order to evaluate
possible solutions or to mitigate potentially damaging impacts.

**Allocation of funds**: to determine how funds are distributed, so that they are allocated
properly against need and underpin local service delivery.

**Conceptual**: to help understand the key influences that are important to a system being
modelled. A variety of problem-structuring techniques are used to develop conceptual models.

**The type is not a seventh impact dimension.** You do not score it. What it gives you is a check
on the six you have just scored: a model that allocates funds and a model that structures a concept
carry very different consequences when they are wrong, so if your allocation model is not scoring
highly on decision and finance, look again.

A model can be Business Critical whatever its type. That is decided by the impact it carries rather
than by where it sits in this list. See
[section 8](../08-business-critical/index.qmd).[^src-govs-010-section-6-11]

## When you disagree

If the commissioner and the analyst do not agree on the level, the Analytical Quality and Assurance
Lead decides.

## When there is not enough time

Sometimes there genuinely is not. Where time and resource constraints mean it is not possible to do
as much assurance as would be desirable, addressing the areas of greatest risk should take priority,
and you should inform the commissioner how you addressed the risks, what risks remain, and the
caveats that go with them.[^src-aqua-book-section-3-2]

**NHSBSA's own sheet answers this.** Level 1 checks are for low risk analyses "and when there is
very limited time to carry out assurance", and Level 2 is for moderate risk analyses "and for
analyses with very limited time, if time permits". So the sheet already tells you what to drop to
and in what order, rather than leaving it to the moment.

**The order of preference is: reduce the scope of the question, not the assurance applied to the
answer.** A narrower question answered properly is more useful than a broad one answered
unreliably, and it is usually possible.

Where even that is not possible:

- prioritise the highest-risk checks and complete those
- state plainly in the output which assurance was not carried out
- say what that means for how the analysis can and cannot be used

Where time constraints mean insufficient assurance has taken place, that should be explicitly
acknowledged and reported in the assurance statement, along with the known limitations and
conditions that follow from it.[^src-aqua-book-chapter-4] The assurance statement is in
[section 6](../06-doing-the-work/index.qmd).

What is not acceptable is quietly recording a lower level, so that the assurance you skipped never
appears to have been needed. That is the difference between a constraint and a cover-up.

## Business Critical analysis

{{< include /guidance/_partials/bca-assurance-level.qmd >}}

[Section 8](/guidance/08-business-critical/index.qmd) gathers the whole of what being Business

## Recording your decision

Record the level, the date, and who agreed it, in the specification you agree with your
commissioner. The analyst writes that specification and shares it with the commissioner for sign
off.[^src-aqua-book-section-6-1-2] The guidance also asks for the completed sheet to be saved and
attached to the Specification.[^src-bca-assurance-journey-s5] At Level 2 the
analyst and commissioner agree the level together. At Level 3 and Level 4 the Analytical Quality and
Assurance Lead confirms it.

That record is what makes proportionate assurance auditable rather than something reconstructed
afterwards. It is also, in practice, the thing that protects you: it shows the judgement was made
deliberately, at the right time, on stated grounds.

**Set the level at scoping, not at design.** The specification agreed with the commissioner defines
the level of assurance required[^src-aqua-book-section-6-1-2], and GovS 010 asks for the levels of
quality and certainty required to be agreed and recorded at the same point[^src-govs-010-section-5-2].
Design is where the assurance activities that deliver the level are established and planned [AQuA
Book section 7.1.2], which is a different question and a later one.

The order matters more than it sounds. A level agreed after the method has been chosen cannot change
the method, so it stops being a decision and becomes a label. The Business Critical determination
sits at the same point, and for the same reason.
